concepts_used: Constitutional Position of High Courts: Articles 214–231

solution.concept_anchor: HC as constitutional court not statutory court
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d is deceptive because students familiar with Parliament's legislative power may incorrectly assume that HCs, like many bodies, derive their powers from statute rather than the Constitution itself.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): HCs were not created by the Government of India Act, 1935 — they draw their current constitutional position from Part VI of the Constitution.
Eliminate (b): The description of a 'statutory court' is precisely what a HC is NOT — its powers flow from the Constitution, not from Parliament's legislation.
Eliminate (d): Parliament can establish a common HC under Article 231 for two or more states, but this does not make the HC a statutory court — it remains a constitutional court.
Confirm (c): Because HCs are constitutional courts, their core jurisdiction cannot be entirely abolished by ordinary legislation — this is the critical implication.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap here targets students who conflate 'Parliament can legislate about HCs' with 'HCs are statutory bodies.' Parliament can indeed legislate regarding HCs (e.g., establishing a common HC under Article 231), but the HC's very existence, jurisdiction, and powers flow from Part VI of the Constitution, making it a constitutional court. This distinction has practical consequences: Parliament cannot, by ordinary law, extinguish the core constitutional jurisdiction of a HC, whereas it could modify a purely statutory body's powers freely.
solution.final_explanation:
High Courts derive their existence and powers directly from the Constitution of India (Part VI, Articles 214–231), which makes them constitutional courts, not statutory courts. This distinction is foundational.

• Option (a): Incorrect. While predecessor courts existed under British-era statutes, the current HCs are creatures of the Constitution — their position is defined by Articles 214 onwards.
• Option (b): Incorrect. A statutory court's powers can be freely modified or extinguished by ordinary legislation. This does not apply to HCs whose core jurisdiction is constitutionally entrenched.
• Option (c): Correct. Being a constitutional court means Parliament cannot, through ordinary legislation, completely abrogate the HC's constitutionally granted jurisdiction (especially writ jurisdiction under Article 226).
• Option (d): Incorrect. Article 231 empowers Parliament to create a common HC for two or more states, but this power does not convert HCs into statutory courts.

Value Addition:
• Article 214 mandates one HC per state; Article 231 is the exception permitting a common HC.
• The HC's writ jurisdiction (Article 226) is part of the basic structure per L. Chandra Kumar (1997).
• Constitutional courts have inherent powers not limited to what statutes grant them.

concepts_used: Original Jurisdiction of High Courts

solution.concept_anchor: Original civil jurisdiction — only Charter High Courts

statement_analysis.statement: All High Courts in India possess original civil jurisdiction by virtue of being constitutional courts.
statement_analysis.reason: Original civil jurisdiction (in suits of a specified pecuniary value) belongs only to the three Charter High Courts — Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras — not all HCs.

statement_analysis.statement: Every High Court has original jurisdiction to try election petitions challenging the election of members to the state legislature and Lok Sabha seats within its territorial jurisdiction.
statement_analysis.reason: Under the Representation of the People Act, 1951, election petitions are presented to the HC having jurisdiction over the constituency — this is a form of original jurisdiction available to all HCs.

statement_analysis.statement: The original jurisdiction of High Courts in matters of admiralty, matrimonial, and probate cases is preserved by Article 225 of the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 225 explicitly preserves the existing jurisdiction and law administered by HCs as it stood before the Constitution — this covers admiralty, matrimonial, and testamentary/probate matters for HCs that possessed such jurisdiction.

solution.strong_distractor: d — A student may eliminate all three statements if they confuse the scope of original jurisdiction, wrongly believing only Charter HCs can try any original matter including election petitions.
elimination_logic: Eliminate any option that validates Statement 1 as correct — original civil jurisdiction is not universal; it belongs only to the three Charter HCs (Calcutta, Bombay, Madras).

Confirm Statement 2 as correct — election petitions under the Representation of the People Act, 1951 are filed before the HC of the relevant constituency, giving every HC this form of original jurisdiction.
Confirm Statement 3 as correct — Article 225 is a saving provision preserving pre-Constitution jurisdiction including admiralty, matrimonial, and probate for those HCs that had such powers.
The combination of only Statements 2 and 3 being correct points to option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in Statement 1 exploits the 'scope-extension' technique: students who know that HCs have original jurisdiction (true for some) incorrectly extend it to all HCs. The word 'all' is the trap. Only the Charter HCs — Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras — received original civil jurisdiction via Royal Charters pre-dating the Constitution, preserved under Article 225. A partially prepared student may mark Statement 1 as correct because they recall that HCs 'have original jurisdiction,' missing the crucial qualifier.
solution.final_explanation:
Original jurisdiction of High Courts is not uniform across all HCs — this is one of the most frequently exploited distinctions in UPSC questions.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Original civil jurisdiction in suits above a specified pecuniary value is exclusive to the three Charter High Courts (Calcutta, Bombay, Madras), whose charters pre-date the Constitution. Article 225 preserves this pre-existing jurisdiction but does not extend it to all HCs.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Under Sections 80–81 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, election petitions are presented to the HC of the relevant constituency. This gives every HC original jurisdiction over election disputes — a statutory form of original jurisdiction available universally.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 225 is a constitutional saving clause preserving the jurisdiction (admiralty, matrimonial, probate, testamentary) and law as it existed in HCs immediately before the Constitution came into force.

Value Addition:
• The three Charter HCs can try original suits of Rs. 20 lakh or more (threshold varies by state law).
• HC's jurisdiction over election petitions for Presidential/VP elections does NOT exist — those go directly to the Supreme Court.
• Article 225 also preserves the procedure and rules of courts as they existed before the Constitution.

concepts_used: Appellate Jurisdiction of High Courts: Civil and Criminal

solution.concept_anchor: HC second appeal — only questions of law

statement_analysis.statement: A High Court, in exercising second appellate jurisdiction in civil matters, may re-examine concurrent findings of fact reached by both the trial court and the first appellate court.
statement_analysis.reason: In second appeal, the HC is restricted to questions of law; it ordinarily cannot interfere with concurrent findings of fact arrived at by two courts below — this is a well-established principle under Section 100 CPC.

statement_analysis.statement: A High Court's criminal appellate jurisdiction includes hearing appeals against convictions by Sessions Courts where the sentence imposed is imprisonment for seven years or more.
statement_analysis.reason: The HC's criminal appellate jurisdiction covers appeals from Sessions Courts including convictions involving substantial sentences — seven years or more is among the qualifying thresholds for appeal to the HC.

statement_analysis.statement: There is no distinction between a first appeal and a second appeal before the High Court — both permit the court to examine questions of fact and law equally.
statement_analysis.reason: A first appeal before the HC is a rehearing on both fact and law; a second appeal is confined to substantial questions of law — the distinction is fundamental under the CPC and criminal procedure.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who correctly identify Statement 1 as wrong may accept Statement 3 as correct due to general belief that HCs can always look at both fact and law, missing the crucial first-appeal vs. second-appeal distinction.
elimination_logic: Identify Statement 1 as incorrect — in second appeal, the HC cannot re-examine concurrent findings of fact; it is limited to questions of law under Section 100 CPC.
Identify Statement 2 as correct — HC criminal appellate jurisdiction over Sessions Court convictions with 7+ years is a valid threshold, so Statement 2 is NOT incorrect.
Identify Statement 3 as incorrect — first and second appeals are fundamentally different: first appeal allows examination of both fact and law; second appeal is confined to questions of law.
The question asks which are NOT correct — only Statements 1 and 3 are incorrect, pointing to option (c).
solution.final_explanation:
The appellate jurisdiction of HCs operates differently depending on whether it is a first or second appeal, and whether the matter is civil or criminal.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: In second civil appeal (under Section 100 CPC), the HC is confined to 'substantial questions of law.' Concurrent findings of fact by two lower courts are ordinarily binding on the HC. This is one of the most exploited UPSC traps in appellate jurisdiction questions.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The HC's criminal appellate jurisdiction extends to convictions by Sessions Courts with sentences of seven or more years — this is a proper qualifying threshold.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: A first appeal is a full rehearing where the HC can re-examine both fact and law. A second appeal is restricted to questions of law only. Treating them as equivalent is a fundamental error.

Value Addition:
• Under Section 374 CrPC (now BNSS), an appeal against conviction by a Sessions/Additional Sessions Judge lies to the HC.
• In civil matters, Section 96 CPC governs first appeals; Section 100 CPC governs second appeals.
• 'Substantial question of law' must be specifically formulated by the HC at the admission stage of a second appeal.

Distinction between Article 226 (HC Writs) and Article 32 (SC Writs)

solution.concept_anchor: Article 226 scope wider than Article 32

statement_analysis.statement: Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights only, mirroring the scope of Article 32.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 226 covers 'any purpose' — it is not limited to FR enforcement. This is a broader scope than Article 32, which is confined to FR violations.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 226 jurisdiction of a High Court is suspended during the operation of a National Emergency.
statement_analysis.reason: Unlike Article 32 (which can be suspended during Emergency under Article 359), Article 226 is NOT suspended during a National Emergency — this is a critical constitutional distinction.

statement_analysis.statement: A High Court can issue writs against private bodies if such bodies are performing public functions or duties of a public nature.
statement_analysis.reason: The writ jurisdiction under Article 226 extends to private bodies discharging public functions — this is judicially settled and a feature not shared by ordinary civil remedies.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 32, unlike Article 226, is itself a Fundamental Right and cannot be suspended except during a National Emergency by Presidential order under Article 359.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 32 is guaranteed as a FR under Part III; Article 359 allows suspension of the right to move courts for enforcement of FRs (including Article 32) during Emergency. Article 226 has no such suspension mechanism.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know that Article 226 is broader than Article 32 may still wrongly assume that Emergency suspends both, and may count Statement 2 as correct, inflating the count to three correct statements.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is incorrect — Article 226 covers 'any purpose,' not just Fundamental Rights enforcement. Eliminate any count that treats it as correct.
Statement 2 is incorrect — Article 226 is NOT suspended during National Emergency; only Article 32 can be suspended under Article 359. Eliminate any count that treats it as correct.
Statements 3 and 4 are both correct — private body writs are permissible under Article 226, and Article 32 being a FR subject to Article 359 suspension is accurate.
Only two statements (3 and 4) are correct — the answer is 'Only two,' which is option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the primary trap. Students who know that Emergency restricts access to courts may incorrectly extend this to Article 226 as well. The constitutional reality is precise: Article 359 allows the President to suspend the right to move courts for FR enforcement (Article 32), but Article 226 is a constitutional power of the HC that is not suspended. This was judicially reaffirmed and remains a frequently tested distinction.
solution.final_explanation:
The distinction between Articles 226 and 32 is among the most tested areas in UPSC Polity. Consider the four statements:

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Article 226 empowers HCs to issue writs 'for any purpose,' not just FR enforcement. This makes it broader than Article 32, which is exclusively for FR violations.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 226 is not suspended during a National Emergency. Article 359 permits suspension of the right to approach courts under Article 32, but Article 226 continues to operate — this is a constitutionally significant safeguard.
• Statement 3 — Correct: HCs can issue writs against private bodies that perform public functions, e.g., a private university exercising statutory power. This is established jurisprudence under Article 226.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right (making it a guaranteed remedy); it can be suspended under Article 359 during Emergency. Article 226 lacks both these attributes — it is not a FR, cannot be suspended, but can be refused by the HC in its discretion.

Value Addition:
• Whirlpool Corp. v. Registrar of Trade Marks (1998) held that HC writ jurisdiction under Article 226 cannot be ousted by legislation.
• HC can refuse Article 226 writs on grounds of delay, alternative remedy, or laches — no such discretion exists with Article 32.
• Both Article 226 and Article 32 permit issuance of the same five types of writs: habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, certiorari.

Writ Jurisdiction of High Courts under Article 226

solution.concept_anchor: Article 226 vs Article 227 — nature and scope
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who conflate supervisory jurisdiction with appellate jurisdiction may misplace Article 227's reach over military tribunals and match it incorrectly.
elimination_logic: Match A (Article 226) with 3 (writ jurisdiction for any purpose, including against private bodies performing public functions) — this is definitionally accurate for Article 226.
Match B (Article 227) with 1 (superintendence over all courts and tribunals except military tribunals) — the exclusion of military tribunals is the specific limitation under Article 227.
Match C (Article 32) with 4 (FR enforcement only, itself a Fundamental Right) — Article 32 is exclusively for FR enforcement and is itself guaranteed as a FR.

Match D (Article 215) with 2 (Court of Record with inherent power to punish contempt) — Article 215 declares every HC a Court of Record with contempt powers; this eliminates options (a), (c), and (d), confirming option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap conflates Articles 226 and 227. Students know both are HC powers and may match Article 227 with 'writs against private bodies' (List II item 3), not realising that writs against private bodies is a feature of Article 226 (writ jurisdiction), not Article 227 (supervisory jurisdiction). Article 227 extends to courts and tribunals (excluding military) but is administrative/supervisory in character, not writ-issuing. Similarly, confusing Article 215 (Court of Record) with Article 226 (writ jurisdiction) is a common error.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests precise knowledge of four distinct constitutional provisions relating to HC powers.

Correct pairings:
• A–3: Article 226 grants HCs power to issue writs 'for any purpose' — not limited to FR enforcement — and this extends to private bodies performing public functions.
• B–1: Article 227 confers superintendence over all courts and tribunals within the HC's territorial jurisdiction, with an explicit exclusion of military tribunals — a critical qualifier.
• C–4: Article 32 is exclusively for enforcing Fundamental Rights and is itself a Fundamental Right under Part III — making access to the Supreme Court for FR enforcement a guaranteed right.
• D–2: Article 215 declares every HC a Court of Record, which entails that its judgments have evidentiary value and it has inherent power to punish for contempt of court.

The trap pairing is A–1 (confusing Article 226 with Article 227's supervisory reach) or D–3 (confusing Court of Record powers with writ jurisdiction).

Value Addition:
• Article 227 cannot be used as a disguised form of appellate jurisdiction — the HC can only correct jurisdictional errors, not re-decide the merits.
• Military courts/tribunals are excluded from HC's supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 — a frequently tested exclusion.
• Article 215 and Article 129 (SC as Court of Record) are parallel provisions for HC and SC respectively.

meta.subject: Polity
concepts_used: Power of Judicial Review in High Courts

solution.concept_anchor: HC cannot strike down law on DPSP alone — needs FR violation
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know that DPSPs are important constitutional directives may wrongly assume that violation of a DPSP alone is enough for HC to strike down legislation, and choose (a) believing both A and R are linked.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is A correct? — Yes. A HC can indeed strike down state legislation that violates Fundamental Rights under Part III. This is a core function of judicial review.

Step 2: Is R correct? — No. The Reason states that DPSPs are enforceable in courts if they conflict with Fundamental Rights. This is factually incorrect — DPSPs are explicitly non-justiciable under Article 37; a HC cannot strike down legislation merely because it violates a DPSP.
Step 3: Since R is factually incorrect, the answer must be (c): A is correct, R is incorrect.
Confirm: correct_option is (c) — A is correct but R is incorrect.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap uses reversed causation. Students know that Fundamental Rights prevail over DPSPs when in conflict (as settled in State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan, 1951). The Reason cleverly inverts this — implying DPSPs are enforceable against FRs. A partially prepared student who recalls that 'DPSPs and FRs have a complex relationship' may mark R as correct. The precise constitutional position is that DPSPs are expressly non-justiciable (Article 37) and a HC cannot invalidate legislation on the ground of DPSP violation alone; there must be a FR violation.
solution.final_explanation:
Judicial review by High Courts is anchored in Fundamental Rights enforcement, not DPSP compliance.

Assertion (A): Correct. A HC possesses the power to strike down state legislation that violates Fundamental Rights in Part III. This is the essence of constitutional judicial review and flows from Article 226 and the HC's status as a constitutional court.

Reason (R): Incorrect. Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSPs) under Part IV are explicitly declared non-justiciable by Article 37 — 'the provisions contained in this Part shall not be enforceable by any court.' No court, including a HC, can invalidate legislation merely because it violates a DPSP. The HC's power of judicial review requires a violation of Part III (Fundamental Rights) or the constitutional scheme — DPSP violation alone is insufficient.

Causal relationship: Does not arise since R is factually wrong. Answer: (c).

Value Addition:
• Post the 42nd Amendment (1976), Article 31C was expanded to shield laws giving effect to all DPSPs from FR challenges — but the SC in Minerva Mills (1980) struck down this blanket protection.
• HCs can apply the basic structure doctrine to constitutional amendments — not just ordinary legislation.
• A law can be valid even if it restricts a FR, provided it satisfies the conditions of reasonable restriction under Articles 19(2)–19(6).

Contempt Jurisdiction of High Courts

solution.concept_anchor: Contempt of Courts Act 1971 — truth as defence 2006 amendment
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know the Contempt of Courts Act is from 1971 may chronologically misplace the 2006 amendment before the original Act or mix it with other criminal law amendments of the 1990s.
elimination_logic: Anchor the sequence: The Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950 — Article 215 declaring HCs as Courts of Record is the foundational step.
The Contempt of Courts Act was enacted in 1971 — this codified the law of contempt and came after the Constitution but well before the 2006 amendment.
The 2006 amendment introduced 'truth' as a valid defence in criminal contempt proceedings — this is clearly the most recent development in the sequence.
The correct chronological order is: Constitution (1950) → Contempt of Courts Act (1971) → 2006 Amendment, which corresponds to option (d): P → Q → R.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal trap lies in the 2006 amendment. Students who recall that 'truth is a defence in contempt' may associate it with the original 1971 Act rather than recognising it as a 2006 amendment — potentially reversing R and Q in the sequence. Additionally, some students may confuse the 1971 Act with the 1952 Contempt of Courts Act that preceded it, creating further temporal confusion.
solution.final_explanation:
The law of contempt of court in India has evolved through three key developments in chronological order.

P — Article 215 of the Constitution (1950): Declared every HC a Court of Record with inherent power to punish for contempt. This is the constitutional foundation of contempt jurisdiction.

Q — Contempt of Courts Act, 1971: Parliament codified the law of contempt, defining civil contempt (wilful disobedience of court orders) and criminal contempt (scandalising the court, prejudicing fair trial). This Act governs proceedings but does not displace the HC's constitutional contempt power.

R — 2006 Amendment to the Contempt of Courts Act: This amendment introduced 'truth' as a valid defence in criminal contempt proceedings, provided the statement was made in public interest and publication was in good faith. This was a significant liberalisation.

Correct sequence: P → Q → R (option d).

Value Addition:
• A 1952 Contempt of Courts Act existed before the 1971 Act — the 1971 Act replaced it with a more comprehensive framework.
• Civil contempt requires wilful disobedience; criminal contempt can include acts outside court premises that scandalise the court.
• The Supreme Court's contempt power flows from Article 129 (parallel to Article 215 for HCs).

concepts_used: Jurisdiction over Tribunals and the HC–Tribunal Interface

solution.concept_anchor: L. Chandra Kumar — HC review over tribunals is basic structure
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who remember that Articles 323A and 323B allow Parliament to create tribunals may assume Parliament can also entirely exclude HC jurisdiction — option (c) makes this plausible by citing the correct articles.
elimination_logic: Identify the legal issue: Can Parliament exclude HC judicial review over a statutory tribunal's orders entirely?
Eliminate (a): The scenario does not concern military tribunals — the exclusion in (a) conflates Article 227's military tribunal exception with this entirely different issue.

Eliminate (c): While Articles 323A and 323B do permit creation of tribunals and exclusion clauses, L. Chandra Kumar (1997) held such exclusion of HC jurisdiction unconstitutional — (c) states the opposite of settled law.

Eliminate (d): The SC's Special Leave jurisdiction under Article 136 is separate — the question is about HC jurisdiction, not SC's power; (d) is a distractor invoking a real but inapplicable provision.

Confirm (b): L. Chandra Kumar (1997) expressly held that HC jurisdiction under Articles 226/227 over tribunal orders is part of the basic structure of the Constitution and cannot be excluded by Parliament.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap in option (c) is sophisticated: it cites the correct constitutional articles (323A and 323B) which genuinely empower Parliament to create tribunals and originally contained exclusion clauses for HC jurisdiction. A student who recalls that these articles exist and permit exclusion — without knowing that L. Chandra Kumar overruled the exclusion as unconstitutional — will confidently choose (c). The trap exploits partial knowledge of the constitutional provisions without the judicial correction.
solution.final_explanation:
The interface between High Courts and statutory tribunals is governed by the landmark judgment in L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997).

The scenario presents a Parliament-enacted statute creating a specialised service tribunal and explicitly barring High Court jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227 over its orders. The constitutional question: is such exclusion valid?

Applicable principle: L. Chandra Kumar (1997) — The Supreme Court (7-judge bench) held that the power of judicial review over tribunal orders vested in HCs under Articles 226 and 227 forms part of the basic structure of the Constitution. No parliamentary legislation can exclude this jurisdiction.

• Option (a): Incorrect. The exclusion of military tribunals is a feature of Article 227 (supervisory jurisdiction) and is irrelevant to this scenario involving a civilian service tribunal.
• Option (b): Correct. L. Chandra Kumar settled that HC jurisdiction under Articles 226/227 cannot be excluded — all tribunal orders must remain subject to HC scrutiny.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Though Articles 323A and 323B originally permitted such exclusion, L. Chandra Kumar declared those exclusion clauses unconstitutional as violating the basic structure.
• Option (d): Incorrect. Article 136 (Special Leave to SC) operates independently; its existence does not substitute for or displace HC jurisdiction.

Value Addition:
• L. Chandra Kumar overruled S.P. Sampath Kumar v. Union of India (1987), which had upheld exclusion of HC jurisdiction.
• Tribunals under Articles 323A and 323B can be established but their orders must go to a Division Bench of the HC, not directly to the SC.
• The basic structure doctrine was first enunciated in Kesavananda Bharati (1973).

concepts_used: Transfer of Cases between High Courts and Supreme Court

solution.concept_anchor: Article 228 — HC withdraws case; Article 139A — SC transfers
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students may confuse Article 139A (SC's power to transfer from one HC to another) with Article 228 (HC's own withdrawal power), and eliminate (b) thinking it incorrectly describes Article 228.
elimination_logic: Identify the common attribute across three options: powers of the High Court to deal with cases involving constitutional questions — Article 228 withdrawal, inherent powers, and certificate jurisdiction all belong to the HC.
Option (c) describes a transfer power vested in the Supreme Court (Article 139A) — the SC transfers cases from one HC to another or from an HC to itself.

Options (a), (b), and (d) all describe HC-level powers: withdrawing subordinate court cases (Article 228), issuing writs for constitutional questions (Article 226), and certifying cases for SC appeal (Article 134A) respectively.
The odd one out is (c) — it is an SC power, not an HC power, making it the item that does not belong to the same category as the others.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap places an SC power (Article 139A transfer) among HC powers. Students who know that 'cases can be transferred between courts' may associate this with the HC's own withdrawal power under Article 228, failing to distinguish who holds the transfer power. Article 228 gives the HC the power to withdraw from subordinate courts; Article 139A gives the SC the power to transfer between HCs or from HC to SC. Confusing the subject of the power is the classic entity-swap trap.
solution.final_explanation:
Three of the four options describe powers exercised by High Courts; one describes a power of the Supreme Court.

• Option (a): HC's own power — Article 228 empowers an HC to withdraw a case from a subordinate court if a substantial question of constitutional law arises, decide that question itself, and return the case or dispose it.
• Option (b): HC's own power — Article 226 allows the HC to issue writs including for enforcement of constitutional rights, which may arise in cases involving constitutional questions.
• Option (c): NOT an HC power — The power to transfer cases from one HC to another HC, or from an HC to the Supreme Court, is vested in the Supreme Court under Article 139A. The HC has no such transfer power over other HCs.
• Option (d): HC's own power — Article 134A empowers an HC to certify (on its own motion or on application) a case for appeal to the Supreme Court on constitutional or other questions.

Value Addition:
• Article 228 transfers are to the HC itself — the HC then sends the case back after resolving the constitutional question, or disposes it entirely.
• Article 139A was inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976) — giving SC explicit transfer powers.
• Transfer under Article 139A can be initiated by the SC on its own motion or on application.

meta.subject: Polity
concepts_used: High Court's Power of Certification under Article 132, 133, and 134A

solution.concept_anchor: Article 133 certificate — substantial question of law of general importance

statement_analysis.statement: A High Court may, under Article 134A, certify any civil case decided by it for appeal to the Supreme Court, regardless of the nature or importance of the legal question involved.
statement_analysis.reason: Certification under Article 133 (for civil cases) requires that the case involves a 'substantial question of law of general importance' — not every civil case qualifies. Article 134A merely provides the procedural mechanism for the HC to grant or grant on application such certificates; the substantive threshold under Articles 132 and 133 still applies.

statement_analysis.statement: Even when a High Court refuses to grant a certificate of fitness for appeal to the Supreme Court, the aggrieved party may seek Special Leave to Appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 136 grants the Supreme Court plenary discretionary power to grant Special Leave to appeal from any judgment or order of any court or tribunal — this is an independent and overriding remedy that operates regardless of HC's decision to certify or refuse.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know that Article 134A allows HCs to certify cases may infer that both statements are correct, not spotting that Statement 1 removes the essential threshold of 'substantial question of law of general importance.'
elimination_logic: Test Statement 1: Article 134A is a procedural article — the substantive conditions for certification are in Articles 132 (constitutional question) and 133 (substantial question of law of general importance in civil cases). Not every civil case qualifies — Statement 1 is incorrect.

Test Statement 2: Article 136 is the SC's plenary Special Leave power — it operates independently of whether the HC certified the case. A refusal by the HC does not bar an Article 136 petition — Statement 2 is correct.
With Statement 1 incorrect and Statement 2 correct, the answer must be (d): Statement 1 incorrect, Statement 2 correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Certification of cases by the HC for appeal to the SC operates on distinct substantive thresholds under different articles.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Article 134A provides the procedural mechanism (HC may certify on its own motion or on application) but the substantive conditions are set by Articles 132 and 133. For civil appeals (Article 133), the HC must certify that the case involves a 'substantial question of law of general importance' the decision of which by the SC is necessary. Not every civil case decided by the HC can be certified — the threshold is meaningful and limits access.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Article 136 is the Supreme Court's residual, plenary, discretionary jurisdiction to grant Special Leave to appeal from any court or tribunal. The HC's refusal to grant a certificate does not foreclose this remedy. The aggrieved party can directly petition the SC under Article 136.

Value Addition:
• For criminal appeals (Article 134), the HC must certify the case is fit for appeal — typically for acquittals reversed to conviction, or sentences of death certified by HC.
• Article 132 covers constitutional questions from all three court types (civil, criminal, other).
• Special Leave under Article 136 is discretionary — the SC can refuse without giving reasons.

meta.subject: Polity
concepts_used: Territorial Jurisdiction and Seat of High Courts

solution.concept_anchor: President decides seat of HC — not state government
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know that state governments have significant roles in matters of HCs (e.g., through the Governor in judge appointments) may incorrectly attribute the decision on seat to the state government.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The Chief Justice of India plays no constitutional role in deciding the seat (location) of a HC — that is an executive decision under Article 130/related provisions.
Eliminate (c): The state government does not decide the seat of the HC — this is a central executive power.
Eliminate (d): The Judicial Commission for HCs does not exist as a constitutional body with this power.
Confirm (b): The President of India decides the seat of a HC — including when a common HC is established for two or more states under Article 231.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap substitutes 'state government' or 'Governor' — entities genuinely involved in HC administration (e.g., Governor consults in judge appointment) — for 'President,' who actually decides the seat of the HC. Students with partial knowledge of HC governance assign this power to the state government, which has no role in determining the HC's seat.
solution.final_explanation:
The seat of a High Court — the city where it is located — is determined by the President of India, not by the HC itself, the state government, or the judiciary.

• Option (a): Incorrect. The Chief Justice of India is involved in the collegium process for judge appointments but has no constitutional role in fixing the seat of a HC.
• Option (b): Correct. The President of India decides the seat of the HC. This applies both to individual state HCs and to common HCs established for two or more states under Article 231.
• Option (c): Incorrect. The state government has no authority to fix the seat of the HC — states may make demands or recommendations, but the decision vests with the central executive (President).
• Option (d): Incorrect. No constitutional body called a 'Judicial Commission for High Courts' exists with this power.

Value Addition:
• Article 231 allows Parliament to establish a common HC — e.g., Punjab and Haryana HC at Chandigarh.
• The demand for a separate HC for Telangana was resolved in 2019 when the Telangana HC was established.
• The concept of 'circuit benches' involves the HC sitting at locations other than its principal seat — these are also subject to presidential approval.

meta.subject: Polity
concepts_used: Appointment, Removal, and Conditions of Service of HC Judges

solution.concept_anchor: Governor consulted for HC appointments — not for SC

statement_analysis.statement: The Governor of the concerned state is constitutionally required to be consulted in the process of appointing a High Court judge.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 217(1) mandates that the President appoint HC judges in consultation with the CJI, the Chief Justice of the concerned HC, and the Governor of the state — the Governor's consultation is a constitutional requirement specific to HC appointments.

statement_analysis.statement: The process of removing a High Court judge is identical to that of removing a Supreme Court judge — requiring an address by each House of Parliament and a Presidential order.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 217(1)(b) specifies that an HC judge may be removed by the President in the same manner as a SC judge under Article 124(4) — requiring an address by each House of Parliament in the same session with a special majority.

statement_analysis.statement: The collegium for recommending High Court judge appointments consists solely of the Chief Justice of India and the two senior-most judges of the Supreme Court.
statement_analysis.reason: Per the Third Judges Case (1998), the HC collegium for appointments involves the CJI and his four senior-most SC colleagues (for transfers and appointments); additionally, the Chief Justice of the concerned HC is consulted. Limiting it to 'two senior-most SC judges' misrepresents the composition.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know the collegium system involves 'the CJI + senior judges' may accept Statement 3 as correct without recalling the precise number (four, not two), and choose (d) believing all three are correct.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 as correct — Article 217(1) explicitly includes the Governor in the consultation process, a feature absent from SC judge appointments where only the SC collegium is consulted.
Confirm Statement 2 as correct — the removal process for HC judges mirrors that for SC judges precisely: address by both Houses of Parliament with special majority + Presidential order.

Identify Statement 3 as incorrect — the collegium for HC appointments per the Third Judges Case (1998) involves the CJI and four senior-most SC judges, not two. The Chief Justice of the HC is also consulted.
Statements 1 and 2 are correct, Statement 3 is incorrect — option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap in Statement 3 replaces 'four' with 'two' — an easy trap for students who vaguely recall 'CJI + senior judges' without precise knowledge of the Third Judges Case collegium composition. Statement 1 contains the classic 'Governor in HC appointments' trap: students familiar with SC appointments (where the Governor has no role) may think the Governor is irrelevant for HC appointments too — but Article 217 explicitly requires the Governor's consultation for HC appointments.
solution.final_explanation:
Appointment and removal of HC judges involve multiple constitutional actors, and the precise composition differs from SC judge appointments.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 217(1) requires the President to consult the CJI, the Chief Justice of the HC, and the Governor of the state. The Governor's inclusion in HC appointments (but not SC appointments) is a frequently tested constitutional distinction.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Article 217(1)(b) removes an HC judge through the exact mechanism in Article 124(4) — an address by each House of Parliament passed in the same session with a special majority, followed by a Presidential order. Identical to SC removal.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Per the Third Judges Case (1998), the collegium for HC judge recommendations consists of the CJI and his four (not two) senior-most SC colleagues. The Chief Justice of the concerned HC is also consulted, though not part of the collegium formally.

Value Addition:
• The NJAC Act (2014) sought to replace the collegium but was struck down in Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015).
• The Governor's role in HC appointments is consultative, not determinative — the collegium's recommendation is binding post-Second Judges Case.
• HC judges' oath is administered by the Governor of the state.

meta.subject: Polity
concepts_used: Acting, Additional, and Retired Judges of High Courts

solution.concept_anchor: Additional judges Article 224 — cannot be confirmed directly

statement_analysis.statement: An Additional Judge appointed to a High Court under Article 224 may, upon completion of a satisfactory term, be automatically confirmed as a permanent judge of that court without a fresh appointment process.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 224 Additional Judges cannot be directly confirmed as permanent judges — a fresh appointment process under Article 217 is mandatory. There is no automatic confirmation.

statement_analysis.statement: A retired judge of a High Court may be requested to sit and act as a judge of that court with the consent of the President and the retired judge himself under Article 224A.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 224A explicitly allows the Chief Justice of a HC to request a retired judge to sit and act, subject to the consent of both the President and the retired judge — this is accurately described.

statement_analysis.statement: An Acting Chief Justice is appointed under Article 223 whenever the office of the Chief Justice of a High Court is vacant, and such appointment is made by the President.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 223 provides that when the office of the Chief Justice of a HC is vacant or the Chief Justice is absent or unable to perform duties, the President shall appoint one of the other judges as Acting Chief Justice.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know that Additional Judges face some procedural hurdle may believe the question is testing whether Statement 2 or 3 is incorrect, not recognising that Statement 1 contains the only false claim (automatic confirmation).
elimination_logic: Test Statement 1: 'Automatic confirmation' of Additional Judges is the trap — Article 224 sets a maximum term of two years; there is no automatic confirmation. Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Test Statement 2: Article 224A accurately describes retired judges sitting on request with dual consent (President + retired judge). Statement 2 is correct.
Test Statement 3: Article 223 accurately describes Acting Chief Justice appointment by the President when the CJ post is vacant or the CJ is unavailable. Statement 3 is correct.
Only Statement 1 is NOT correct — the answer is (c): 1 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap in Statement 1 contains a real provision (Additional Judges under Article 224 do serve a term) but adds a false element ('automatic confirmation'). A student who knows that Additional Judges are eventually appointed as permanent judges — which often happens in practice — may assume the Constitution permits automatic confirmation, missing the procedural requirement of a fresh appointment. In reality, many Additional Judges do become permanent, but through fresh Article 217 appointments, not through automatic confirmation.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 223, 224, and 224A deal with three distinct categories of non-regular HC judges.

• Statement 1 — NOT Correct: Article 224 permits appointment of Additional Judges for a maximum period of two years to handle temporary increases in the work of a HC. At the end of this term, no automatic confirmation is possible — a fresh appointment under Article 217 is constitutionally required. This is the only incorrect statement.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Article 224A enables the Chief Justice of a HC to request a retired HC or SC judge to sit and act, provided both the President and the retired judge consent. The retired judge receives the same allowances as an appointed judge during this period.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 223 empowers the President to appoint an Acting Chief Justice from among the sitting judges of the HC whenever the Chief Justice's position is vacant or the Chief Justice is unable to perform duties due to absence or otherwise.

Value Addition:
• Article 224 also covers 'Acting Judges' appointed to fill the place of a regular judge temporarily absent — distinct from Additional Judges.
• Additional Judges under Article 224 cannot be converted to permanent without a fresh collegium recommendation and Presidential appointment.
• Article 224A appointments are relatively rare and are used to clear backlogs in specific HCs.

concepts_used: Independence of High Courts: Salaries, Tenure, and Transfer

solution.concept_anchor: HC judges salaries — State Consolidated Fund not Union
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know that SC judges' salaries come from the Union Consolidated Fund (Article 112) may incorrectly apply the same rule to HC judges, making (a) appear correct.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): SC judges' salaries are charged to the Union Consolidated Fund — but HC judges' salaries are charged to the State Consolidated Fund. The entity is swapped.
Eliminate (c): Transfer of HC judges is by Presidential order under Article 222, which requires consultation with the CJI — not 'at the discretion of the Governor.'
Eliminate (d): HC judges are removed through the same Parliamentary address process as SC judges — not by the President alone on advice of the Council of Ministers.

Confirm (b): HC judges' salaries are charged to the Consolidated Fund of the concerned State (Article 229 read with relevant provisions) — not subject to vote in the state legislature, ensuring judicial independence.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The classic entity-swap trap: SC judges' salaries → Union Consolidated Fund; HC judges' salaries → State Consolidated Fund. Students who generalise from SC to HC without remembering this distinction will choose (a). The distinction is constitutionally significant — HC judges' salaries come from the state because HCs are state institutions, but since they are 'charged' (not voted), the state legislature cannot threaten judicial independence by withholding salary appropriations.
solution.final_explanation:
The financial independence of HC judges is secured through constitutional provisions on salary and removal.

• Option (a): Incorrectly matched. SC judges' salaries are charged to the Consolidated Fund of India (Union). HC judges' salaries are charged to the Consolidated Fund of the concerned State — not the Union. This pair swaps the entities.
• Option (b): Correctly matched. HC judges' salaries are charged to the State's Consolidated Fund — this means they are non-votable and cannot be reduced or withheld by the state legislature, protecting judicial independence.
• Option (c): Incorrectly matched. Transfers of HC judges are effected by the President under Article 222 in consultation with the CJI — whose recommendation is binding (post-Second Judges Case). The Governor has no role in transfers.
• Option (d): Incorrectly matched. HC judges can only be removed through an address by both Houses of Parliament (special majority) and a Presidential order — the same procedure as for SC judges. The Council of Ministers cannot advise removal of HC judges unilaterally.

Value Addition:
• Article 222 mandates consultation with CJI for HC judge transfers — this consultation is binding, not merely advisory.
• Charging salaries to the Consolidated Fund (rather than making them subject to vote) is a standard constitutional device to protect institutional independence.
• Administrative expenses of the HC are also charged to the State Consolidated Fund.

(c) Transfer of High Court judges — Effected at the discretion of the Governor of the state in consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court

meta.subject: Polity
concepts_used: High Court's Jurisdiction over Election Disputes

solution.concept_anchor: Article 329 bars HC during election; Presidential election disputes to SC

statement_analysis.statement: Article 329 of the Constitution bars High Courts from entertaining writ petitions challenging any step taken or order made during an ongoing election process.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 329 is a constitutional bar on courts — including HCs — from interfering in electoral matters during the election process itself. The remedy post-election is the election petition before the HC.

statement_analysis.statement: After an election to the state legislature is concluded, disputes regarding the validity of that election must be presented as election petitions before the concerned High Court under the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
statement_analysis.reason: Post-election disputes for state legislature and Lok Sabha elections within a state's territorial jurisdiction are brought before the HC under the RPA 1951 — this is the correct forum for post-election scrutiny.

statement_analysis.statement: Disputes relating to the election of the President and Vice-President of India are also adjudicated by the High Court of Delhi, being the capital's court.
statement_analysis.reason: Presidential and Vice-Presidential election disputes go directly to the Supreme Court of India — not to any HC, including the Delhi HC. This is provided under Article 71 read with the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students may reasonably assume the Delhi HC has special jurisdiction as the capital court and mark Statement 3 as correct, choosing option (c) which includes all three.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 as correct — Article 329 is a clear constitutional bar that applies even to HC writ jurisdiction during the subsistence of an election process.
Confirm Statement 2 as correct — RPA 1951 routes post-election disputes for state legislature and Lok Sabha to the HC having jurisdiction over the constituency.
Identify Statement 3 as incorrect — Presidential and VP election disputes go to the Supreme Court (Article 71), not to any HC. The 'capital court' principle does not exist in constitutional law.
Statements 1 and 2 are correct, Statement 3 is incorrect — option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 exploits the scope-extension trap — students who know that HCs have original jurisdiction over election disputes extend this principle incorrectly to Presidential/VP elections. The Delhi HC has no special status as the 'capital court' for election disputes. The Constitution explicitly routes Presidential and VP election disputes to the Supreme Court under Article 71. A student unfamiliar with Article 71 may plausibly believe that since the President's election has national character, the most prominent HC (Delhi) handles it.
solution.final_explanation:
Election disputes before High Courts are governed by a carefully delineated constitutional and statutory framework.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 329 creates a constitutional bar — no court (including HCs) can interfere during the election process itself via writ jurisdiction. The bar is absolute during the subsistence of the election; HC writ jurisdiction is effectively suspended for electoral interference.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Post-election disputes for state assembly and Lok Sabha seats are channelled to the HC having territorial jurisdiction over the constituency, under Sections 80–81 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. This is the HC's original jurisdiction in election matters.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Article 71 of the Constitution vests jurisdiction over Presidential and Vice-Presidential election disputes exclusively in the Supreme Court. The Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952 reinforces this. No HC — including Delhi — has jurisdiction over these disputes.

Value Addition:
• Article 329(b) bars election petitions except in the form prescribed by law — meaning only the RPA procedure is valid, not a simple writ.
• The Election Commission's orders during elections are generally insulated from judicial interference under Article 329.
• HC cannot grant a stay on election results pending an election petition without very strong prima facie grounds — courts are cautious.

meta.subject: Polity
concepts_used: High Court's Jurisdiction over Subordinate Courts: Control and Inspection

solution.concept_anchor: Article 235 HC control vs Article 233 Governor appointment
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is A correct? — Yes. Article 235 vests control over district courts and subordinate courts (posting, promotion, leave, service matters) in the High Court — not the Governor or state government.

Step 2: Is R correct? — No. The Reason states that 'the Governor appoints district judges without any role for the High Court.' This is factually wrong — Article 233 requires the Governor to appoint district judges in consultation with the High Court. The HC's consultation is constitutionally mandatory.
Step 3: Since R is factually incorrect, the answer is (c): A is correct but R is incorrect.
Confirm: correct_option is (c) — matches the final step.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation trap misrepresents the Governor-HC relationship in judicial appointments. Students who know that 'the Governor appoints district judges' (true) may not recall that this appointment is made in consultation with the HC (mandatory under Article 233). The Reason removes the HC's role entirely — which is false. A partially prepared student accepts R because the Governor's appointment role is real, missing the crucial 'in consultation with HC' qualifier.
solution.final_explanation:
The control of subordinate judiciary is split between two constitutional authorities — the HC and the Governor — but in distinct domains.

Assertion (A): Correct. Article 235 places control over district courts and subordinate courts in the HC. This control covers service matters: posting, promotion, grant of leave, and other conditions of service of judicial officers. The state government (executive) cannot direct the judiciary in these matters — the HC's superintendence is constitutionally guaranteed.

Reason (R): Incorrect. Article 233 governs the appointment of district judges. It requires the Governor to make appointments of district judges in consultation with the HC having jurisdiction over that state. The HC's consultation is not optional — it is constitutionally mandated. The Reason's claim that the Governor acts 'without any role for the High Court' directly contradicts Article 233.

Causal link: Does not arise since R is factually wrong. Answer: (c).

Value Addition:
• The dual authority (Governor appoints, HC controls) over subordinate judiciary frequently causes friction in practice — service disputes often end up before HCs.
• Article 234 covers recruitment to judicial service below the rank of district judge — in this, the state Public Service Commission is involved alongside the HC.
• HC's control under Article 235 extends to judicial officers of the state cadre (not administrative officers).

meta.subject: Polity
concepts_used: Public Interest Litigation (PIL) in High Courts

solution.concept_anchor: HC PIL — territorial limit still applies
solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who recall that HCs can entertain PILs on a wide range of public interest matters may assume there are no territorial restrictions, choosing (d) which suggests an HC can address any central government action.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): PIL before the HC does not require the petitioner to be directly aggrieved — relaxation of locus standi is the defining feature of PIL jurisprudence.
Eliminate (c): PIL can be filed before both the HC (Article 226) and the SC (Article 32) — stating that HCs are not competent for PILs is incorrect.

Eliminate (d): An HC cannot entertain a PIL challenging a central government action that has no territorial nexus with its jurisdiction — the cause of action or the effect of the action must fall within the HC's territory.

Confirm (b): The territorial limit of HC jurisdiction applies even in PIL — an HC cannot address matters with no nexus to its territorial jurisdiction, even if the petitioner frames it as a public interest matter.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap is applied to territorial jurisdiction in PIL. Students who know that PIL relaxes locus standi (standing to sue) may extend this relaxation to territorial jurisdiction — assuming that 'public interest' erases the territorial limit. This is incorrect. The HC's territorial jurisdiction under Article 226 is determined by where the cause of action arises or where the authority against which relief is sought is located. PIL relaxes 'who can file' but not 'where it can be filed.'
solution.final_explanation:
PIL under Article 226 before High Courts is a significant instrument of judicial activism, but it operates within constitutional constraints.

• Option (a): Incorrect. PIL by definition relaxes the traditional locus standi requirement — any public-spirited person can file on behalf of those unable to approach the court. Requiring direct personal grievance defeats the PIL concept.
• Option (b): Correct. Even in PIL, the HC's territorial jurisdiction under Article 226 applies. A PIL challenging a central government action that has no nexus — neither cause of action nor effect — with the HC's territory cannot be maintained before that HC. The territorial limit is a structural constraint on HC jurisdiction.
• Option (c): Incorrect. HCs are fully competent to entertain PILs under Article 226. The SC's PIL jurisdiction under Article 32 coexists with HC PIL — both are valid forums.
• Option (d): Incorrect. An HC cannot entertain a PIL against central government action lacking territorial connection to its jurisdiction — pan-India actions must either have a local nexus or go to the Supreme Court.

Value Addition:
• The Supreme Court has issued guidelines to prevent frivolous PILs — courts can dismiss PILs with costs.
• Environmental PILs before HCs have led to significant regulatory directions — these are within HC territorial reach.
• A PIL filed before one HC cannot be treated as filed before all HCs — each HC exercises jurisdiction only over its territory.

meta.subject: Polity
concepts_used: Inherent Powers of High Courts

solution.concept_anchor: Section 482 CrPC inherent power vs Article 226 writ power

statement_analysis.statement: The inherent power of the High Court to quash FIRs and criminal proceedings — currently embodied in Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure — is a statutory power distinct from its writ jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 482 CrPC (now mirrored in BNSS) is a statutory provision preserving inherent powers of the HC as a superior court of record — it is distinct from the constitutional writ power under Article 226, though both may be invoked to secure similar ends.

statement_analysis.statement: The inherent power of a High Court under Section 482 CrPC is unlimited and can be exercised to override any specific statutory provision, including express bars on jurisdiction.
statement_analysis.reason: Inherent powers are not unlimited — they cannot override specific statutory provisions or express jurisdictional bars. Courts have consistently held that inherent powers exist to prevent abuse of process but cannot circumvent clear legislative prohibitions.

solution.strong_distractor: a — No, (a) is actually the correct answer — the distractor risk is that students conflate inherent powers with constitutional writ powers (treating them as identical), leading them to say Statement 1 is incorrect.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Section 482 CrPC inherent powers are statutory in origin — they preserve inherent powers of the HC as a superior court, but they are triggered by statute, not directly by the Constitution. They are distinct from (though complementary to) Article 226. Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: The claim that inherent powers are 'unlimited' and can override 'any statutory provision' is a classic overstatement — established jurisprudence holds inherent powers cannot override specific statutory provisions or express bars. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — the answer is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap equates inherent statutory powers (Section 482) with constitutional writ powers (Article 226). Students who know that HCs are 'superior courts' with broad powers may conflate these two distinct sources of power, or may assume inherent powers are unlimited since they flow from the court's superior status. The precise position is: inherent powers are extensive but bounded — they secure ends of justice and prevent abuse but cannot override express statutory prohibitions.
solution.final_explanation:
High Courts exercise powers from two distinct sources: constitutional (Article 226, 227) and statutory-inherent (Section 482 CrPC / BNSS equivalent).

• Statement 1 — Correct: Section 482 CrPC preserves the inherent powers of the HC as a court of superior jurisdiction. These powers — to prevent abuse of process, secure ends of justice, give effect to orders — are statutory in their formal basis (Section 482) but rooted in the HC's character as a superior court of record. They are separate from and complementary to Article 226 writ powers. A petitioner may choose either route or both simultaneously.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The HC's inherent powers are not a blank cheque. Courts have consistently held that inherent powers cannot be invoked to circumvent specific statutory provisions, override express legislative prohibitions, or substitute for appellate remedies. They operate in the spaces not occupied by specific statutory provisions, not against them.

Value Addition:
• The Bhartiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023 replaces CrPC — the equivalent of Section 482 is preserved in the new code.
• HC can quash an FIR under Section 482 even if no trial has begun — this is a pre-trial remedy not available before the trial court.
• Article 226 and Section 482 CrPC can be invoked simultaneously in appropriate cases, though courts prefer one route at a time.

solution.concept_anchor: HC contempt extends to subordinate courts — not just itself

statement_analysis.statement: A High Court's contempt jurisdiction under Article 215 extends only to punishing contempt of the High Court itself — it cannot punish contempt of subordinate courts within its jurisdiction.
statement_analysis.reason: The HC's contempt power as a Court of Record extends to contempt of subordinate courts within its jurisdiction — not merely its own contempt. This is a specific characteristic of the HC's supervisory and contempt jurisdiction.

statement_analysis.statement: Civil contempt of court consists of wilful disobedience of any judgment, decree, order, writ, or other process of the court.
statement_analysis.reason: The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 defines civil contempt as wilful disobedience of any judgment, decree, direction, order, writ, or other process of a court — this is an accurate and complete description.

statement_analysis.statement: The 2006 amendment to the Contempt of Courts Act introduced 'truth' as a complete and absolute defence in all categories of contempt proceedings before High Courts.
statement_analysis.reason: Truth is a defence introduced by the 2006 amendment but only in criminal contempt proceedings, and it is subject to conditions: the statement must be in public interest and the publication must be in good faith. It is not an absolute or universal defence in all contempt categories.

statement_analysis.statement: Criminal contempt of court includes actions that tend to scandalise the court or prejudice the fair trial of a case pending before the court.
statement_analysis.reason: Under the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, criminal contempt includes (i) scandalising the court, (ii) prejudicing fair trial of a pending case, and (iii) interfering with the administration of justice — this description is accurate.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who identify Statements 2 and 4 as clearly correct may incorrectly assume Statement 3 is also correct (truth as a complete defence), leading them to count three correct statements.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is incorrect — HC contempt jurisdiction extends to contempt of subordinate courts, not just itself. Eliminate any count treating Statement 1 as correct.
Statement 2 is correct — wilful disobedience definition of civil contempt is textbook accurate.

Statement 3 is incorrect — truth is a defence only in criminal contempt, and even then subject to conditions (public interest, good faith). 'Complete and absolute defence in all categories' is a scope-extension fabrication.
Statement 4 is correct — scandalising the court and prejudicing fair trial are standard components of criminal contempt definition. Only two statements (2 and 4) are correct — answer is (a) Only two.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses a scope-extension trap on the 2006 amendment. Students who know that 'truth was introduced as a defence' in 2006 may not recall the conditions attached — that it applies only in criminal contempt, must be in public interest, and must be in good faith. Calling it 'complete and absolute' and extending it to 'all categories' are the two false extensions. Statement 1 also traps students who conflate contempt of court (restricted to one's own orders) with the HC's actual broader power covering subordinate courts too.
solution.final_explanation:
Contempt jurisdiction of High Courts is multi-layered — it extends beyond the HC's own orders to subordinate courts within its jurisdiction.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: As a Court of Record under Article 215, the HC's contempt jurisdiction extends to contempt of subordinate courts within its territorial jurisdiction, not just contempt of its own orders. This is a direct implication of the HC's supervisory role.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Civil contempt is accurately defined — wilful disobedience of court orders/directions. The key element is 'wilful,' meaning deliberate and not accidental.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Truth as a defence was introduced by the Contempt of Courts (Amendment) Act, 2006, but only for criminal contempt proceedings, and subject to two conditions: (i) it must be in public interest, and (ii) the publication must be in good faith. It is not absolute, and does not apply to civil contempt.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Criminal contempt includes scandalising the court and acts prejudicing fair trial of pending cases — both are established categories under the 1971 Act.

Value Addition:
• Constructive contempt (anticipatory disobedience) is also punishable as civil contempt.
• The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, allows courts to impose imprisonment up to six months or fine up to Rs. 2,000 or both.
• Truth as a defence cannot be used where the motive is malicious or the publication is not bona fide.

concepts_used: Jurisdiction over Tribunals and the HC–Tribunal Interface
Transfer of Cases between High Courts and Supreme Court

solution.concept_anchor: S.P. Sampath Kumar overruled by L. Chandra Kumar 1997
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know L. Chandra Kumar (1997) and Article 139A (42nd Amendment, 1976) may place L. Chandra Kumar before Article 139A in the sequence, reversing the actual order.
elimination_logic: Anchor: Articles 323A and 323B were inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment, 1976 — creating the framework for administrative tribunals.
The 42nd Amendment (1976) predates both Supreme Court cases. Article 139A was also inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
S.P. Sampath Kumar was decided in 1987 — it upheld the exclusion of HC jurisdiction under Article 323A as a valid alternative mechanism.

L. Chandra Kumar was decided in 1997 — it overruled S.P. Sampath Kumar and held exclusion of HC jurisdiction unconstitutional. The correct order is: 42nd Amendment (1976) → S.P. Sampath Kumar (1987) → L. Chandra Kumar (1997), which is P → Q → R = option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal trap involves two Supreme Court cases in the same subject area (tribunal-HC interface) decided a decade apart. Students who know both cases exist but conflate their timeline may place L. Chandra Kumar before Sampath Kumar, or may not know that the 42nd Amendment precedes both. Additionally, some students may confuse S.P. Sampath Kumar (1987) with S.P. Gupta (1982) — another prominent SC case on judicial appointments — creating further temporal confusion.
solution.final_explanation:
The evolution of HC jurisdiction over tribunals followed a three-step trajectory.

P — 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976: Inserted Articles 323A and 323B, empowering Parliament and state legislatures to establish administrative tribunals and exclude HC jurisdiction in their favour. This was the origin of the tribunal-HC conflict.

Q — S.P. Sampath Kumar v. Union of India (1987): The Supreme Court upheld the validity of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 (enacted under Article 323A). It held that the substitution of HC jurisdiction by tribunal jurisdiction was constitutionally valid as an alternative institutional mechanism.

R — L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997): A 7-judge bench overruled S.P. Sampath Kumar. It held that judicial review by HCs under Articles 226/227 forms part of the basic structure of the Constitution and cannot be excluded by Parliament. All tribunal orders must be subject to HC scrutiny.

Correct sequence: P → Q → R = option (d).

Value Addition:
• The Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 (under Article 323A) established the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT).
• Post L. Chandra Kumar, appeals from CAT go to the HC Division Bench, not directly to the SC.
• Article 323B covers tribunals for tax, election disputes, labour, etc. — enacted by both Parliament and state legislatures.

Supervisory Jurisdiction under Article 227

solution.concept_anchor: Article 227 cannot be used as disguised appellate jurisdiction
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know that Article 227 gives the HC supervisory power over all courts and tribunals may assume that it can be used to re-examine the merits of a tribunal's findings, choosing (a).
elimination_logic: Identify the legal issue: A party is invoking Article 227 to have the HC re-examine factual findings of an Industrial Tribunal on merits — is this permissible?
Eliminate (a): Article 227 does not permit the HC to substitute its own findings for those of the tribunal — it is not a vehicle for appellate re-examination of facts or merits.
Eliminate (c): The party is not seeking a writ of certiorari under Article 226 to quash for jurisdictional error — the question is about Article 227 specifically being used for merit review.
Eliminate (d): Article 227 does apply to tribunals (unlike the exclusion for military tribunals) — the issue is not non-applicability to industrial tribunals but the scope of supervisory review.

Confirm (b): Article 227 permits the HC to correct jurisdictional errors, errors apparent on the face of the record, or failure to exercise jurisdiction — but cannot be used as a disguised appellate jurisdiction to re-evaluate factual findings on merits.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges 'supervisory jurisdiction' with 'appellate jurisdiction.' Students who know that Article 227 gives the HC broad superintendence over all courts and tribunals may conflate this supervisory role with an appellate power to re-examine facts and merits. The constitutional position is that Article 227 is a supervisory (not appellate) tool — the HC can correct jurisdictional defects or illegalities but cannot substitute its own assessment of facts for that of the tribunal.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 227 vests the HC with superintendence over all courts and tribunals, but this power has defined boundaries.

The scenario presents a party invoking Article 227 to request the HC to re-examine the factual findings of an Industrial Tribunal on the merits of a wage dispute — essentially seeking appellate review dressed as supervisory oversight.

Applicable principle: Article 227 supervisory jurisdiction is not appellate jurisdiction. The HC can intervene under Article 227 to correct: (i) jurisdictional errors (acting without or in excess of jurisdiction), (ii) errors of law apparent on the face of the record, (iii) refusal to exercise jurisdiction where required. It cannot re-decide facts or substitute its own assessment for that of the tribunal.

• Option (a): Incorrect. The HC cannot use Article 227 to re-examine factual findings on merits and substitute its own conclusion — this would convert supervisory into appellate jurisdiction.
• Option (b): Correct. Article 227 review is confined to jurisdictional errors and errors apparent on the record. Factual re-evaluation on merits is impermissible under Article 227.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Writ of certiorari under Article 226 targets jurisdictional or legal errors leading to quashing — not factual merit re-examination, and the scenario is specifically about Article 227.
• Option (d): Incorrect. Article 227 does apply to industrial and labour tribunals — only military tribunals are excluded from its scope.

Value Addition:
• Article 227 review of a tribunal's decision does not require a legal error on the face of the record as strictly as certiorari — but it still cannot touch concurrent factual findings.
• The HC under Article 227 can also call for records of any subordinate court for examination.
• Article 227 applies even to private arbitral tribunals created by statute, if they discharge public judicial functions.

Territorial Jurisdiction and Seat of High Courts

solution.concept_anchor: Article 214 vs Article 231 — one HC per state vs common HC
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know Article 231 relates to common HCs may pair it with 'one HC per state' (List II item 2) because they associate the article number with HCs generally, without recalling that Article 231 is specifically the exception for common HCs.
elimination_logic: Match A (Article 214) with 2 — Article 214 mandates one HC per state: 'There shall be a High Court for each State.' This is the foundational rule.
Match B (Article 231) with 4 — Article 231 is the Parliament's power to establish a common HC for two or more states — it is the exception to Article 214.
Match C (Article 226) with 1 — Article 226 grants HC power to issue writs 'to any person or authority' for 'any purpose' within its territorial jurisdiction — the widest writ power.

Match D (Article 228) with 3 — Article 228 is specifically the HC's power to withdraw from a subordinate court a case involving a substantial constitutional question. Confirm: option (c) A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap places Articles 214 and 231 in adjacent positions — both relate to the establishment and structure of HCs. A student who knows both articles deal with HCs may swap their distinctive features: Article 214 (one per state) paired with common HC description (List II item 4), and Article 231 paired with 'one HC per state' (List II item 2). The trap exploits the closeness of these provisions in the same chapter of the Constitution.
solution.final_explanation:
Four key articles from Part VI of the Constitution govern the structure and jurisdiction of High Courts.

Correct pairings:
• A–2: Article 214 is the foundational provision — it mandates 'There shall be a High Court for each State,' establishing the one-HC-per-state rule.
• B–4: Article 231 is the exception — it authorises Parliament to establish a common HC for two or more states or union territories. E.g., Punjab and Haryana HC serves both states and Chandigarh UT.
• C–1: Article 226 grants the HC power to issue writs to any person or authority within its territorial jurisdiction 'for any purpose' — not limited to FR enforcement. This broader scope distinguishes it from Article 32.
• D–3: Article 228 enables the HC to withdraw a case from a subordinate court when a substantial question of constitutional law arises — the HC then decides that question, then either disposes the case or returns it to the lower court.

The trap pairings are A–4 (confusing Article 214 with Article 231's subject) and B–2 (the reverse).

Value Addition:
• The Punjab and Haryana HC at Chandigarh is an example of a common HC under Article 231.
• Article 230 allows extension of HC jurisdiction to UTs by Parliament.
• Article 229 covers staff appointments in HCs — Chief Justice controls appointments; salaries charged to State Consolidated Fund.
