solution.concept_anchor: HC judicial review — basic structure applies to constitutional amendments

statement_analysis.statement: A High Court can strike down a state law on the ground that it violates a Directive Principle of State Policy, even without any accompanying violation of a Fundamental Right.
statement_analysis.reason: DPSPs are non-justiciable under Article 37 — courts cannot invalidate legislation solely on the ground of DPSP violation. Judicial review under the HC requires a violation of Fundamental Rights or constitutional provisions, not DPSPs alone.

statement_analysis.statement: A High Court can strike down an executive action of the state government that violates a Fundamental Right even when the action is supported by a resolution of the state legislature.
statement_analysis.reason: HC judicial review extends to executive actions — legislative support for an executive action does not immunise it from judicial scrutiny if it violates Fundamental Rights. Legislative resolutions are not law and provide no additional protection.

statement_analysis.statement: The power of judicial review exercised by a High Court under Article 226 is itself part of the basic structure of the Constitution and cannot be abrogated by constitutional amendment.
statement_analysis.reason: L. Chandra Kumar (1997) held that HC judicial review jurisdiction (Articles 226/227) is part of the basic structure — this implies even a constitutional amendment cannot completely remove this power.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who recall that HCs cannot challenge constitutional amendments directly may doubt Statement 3, choosing option (c) which excludes it, missing the nuanced point that basic structure protection applies.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is incorrect — DPSP violation alone cannot support HC judicial review to strike down law. Article 37 makes DPSPs non-justiciable. Eliminate options validating Statement 1.
Statement 2 is correct — executive actions violating FRs are invalid regardless of legislative support via resolution.
Statement 3 is correct — L. Chandra Kumar specifically held HC judicial review under Articles 226/227 is basic structure — this extends to immunity from constitutional amendment abrogation.
Only Statements 2 and 3 are correct — option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses a subtle scope-extension in reverse — students may think basic structure protection applies only to the SC's review power under Article 32, not to HC's power under Article 226. The L. Chandra Kumar ruling explicitly extended basic structure protection to HC judicial review, making this a nuanced but testable claim. Statement 1 exploits the DPSP-FR confusion trap: students who know DPSPs are important may assume courts can enforce them against state legislation.
solution.final_explanation:
Judicial review by High Courts has both constitutional scope and constitutional protection.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: DPSPs, though foundational to governance, are explicitly declared non-justiciable by Article 37. A HC cannot strike down state legislation solely on the ground that it contravenes a DPSP. Judicial review requires a Fundamental Rights violation or violation of constitutional provisions, not DPSP non-compliance.
• Statement 2 — Correct: HC judicial review of executive actions is not defeated by legislative endorsement in the form of resolutions. Only law enacted by the legislature (not resolutions) can authorise certain restrictions on rights — even then, the law must satisfy constitutional scrutiny. An executive action violating FRs remains invalid regardless of support from a legislature resolution.
• Statement 3 — Correct: L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997) held that HC judicial review jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227 is an integral part of the basic structure. This means Parliament cannot, even by constitutional amendment, completely extinguish HC judicial review — a profound constitutional protection.

Value Addition:
• The basic structure doctrine from Kesavananda Bharati (1973) protects certain core constitutional features — including judicial review — from legislative or amendatory abolition.
• Post-Minerva Mills (1980), blanket protection of DPSP-implementing laws from FR challenge under Article 31C was struck down.
• HC can review administrative orders for violation of natural justice even without a specific FR violation — abuse of power doctrine.

concepts_used: High Court as Court of Record under Article 215

solution.concept_anchor: Court of Record vs original jurisdiction — distinct concepts
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who associate 'Court of Record' with the historical role of courts maintaining records of proceedings may conflate it with original jurisdiction, choosing (a).
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Original civil jurisdiction — the power to try suits at first instance — is not a consequence of being a Court of Record. Only the three Charter HCs have original civil jurisdiction; all HCs are Courts of Record.
Eliminate (c): Being a Court of Record relates to the evidentiary weight of judgments and contempt power — it does not confer appellate jurisdiction, which is separately provided.
Eliminate (d): A Court of Record does not mean the HC's decisions are binding on the Supreme Court — they are binding on subordinate courts but subject to SC's appellate and supervisory jurisdiction.

Confirm (b): The two specific consequences of being a Court of Record under Article 215 are: (i) judgments have evidentiary value and cannot be questioned in subordinate courts, and (ii) the HC has inherent power to punish for contempt of court.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges 'Court of Record' with 'original jurisdiction' — both sound like they involve the HC directly dealing with matters, leading students to associate them. In reality, being a Court of Record is about the legal weight of the HC's judgments and its contempt power, not about its jurisdiction to try original cases. All HCs are Courts of Record; only three have original civil jurisdiction — these are entirely distinct attributes.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 215 declares every High Court to be a 'Court of Record' — a specific legal designation with distinct consequences.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Original civil jurisdiction (to try suits at first instance) is NOT a consequence of Court of Record status. Only the three Charter HCs (Calcutta, Bombay, Madras) have original civil jurisdiction — yet all HCs are Courts of Record. The two concepts are entirely independent.
• Option (b): Correct. Being a Court of Record means: (i) the HC's judgments, proceedings, and acts are of permanent evidentiary value and cannot be questioned in any subordinate court, and (ii) the HC has inherent power to punish for contempt of court.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Appellate jurisdiction is not a consequence of Court of Record status — it is a separately granted jurisdiction under the Constitution and relevant statutes.
• Option (d): Incorrect. HC decisions are binding on subordinate courts within its territorial jurisdiction, but they are not binding on the Supreme Court. The SC can overrule HC judgments in appellate or supervisory proceedings.

Value Addition:
• The Supreme Court is also a Court of Record under Article 129 — parallel to Article 215 for HCs.
• Court of Record status means the records cannot be questioned, contradicted, or impugned in collateral proceedings.
• The HC's contempt power under Article 215 is constitutional in origin — it exists independently of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971.

solution.concept_anchor: HC transfer — Presidential order binding consultation with CJI

statement_analysis.statement: The salaries of High Court judges are charged to the Consolidated Fund of India, ensuring that they are not subject to a vote in Parliament.
statement_analysis.reason: HC judges' salaries are charged to the Consolidated Fund of the concerned State (not the Union/India), making them non-votable in the state legislature — not Parliament. SC judges' salaries come from the Union Consolidated Fund.

statement_analysis.statement: The transfer of a High Court judge from one High Court to another is effected by the President, who must act in consultation with the Chief Justice of India, and post the Second Judges Case, this consultation is binding on the President.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 222 provides for HC judge transfers by Presidential order in consultation with CJI. The Second Judges Case (1993) held this consultation to be binding — the President must act in accordance with the CJI's opinion.

statement_analysis.statement: A High Court judge has no security of tenure — the President may remove a High Court judge at any time on the recommendation of the Council of Ministers without any Parliamentary process.
statement_analysis.reason: HC judges have security of tenure protected by Article 217(1)(b) — removal requires the same parliamentary process as SC judges: an address by each House of Parliament in the same session with a special majority, followed by Presidential order. No executive removal on ministerial advice is possible.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know that 'salaries of judges are charged (non-voted)' may accept Statement 1 as correct without checking which Consolidated Fund — Union or State — applies to HC judges specifically.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is incorrect — HC judges' salaries are charged to the State Consolidated Fund, not the Union/India Consolidated Fund. The fact that they are non-voted is correct but the entity (which fund) is wrong. Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Statement 2 is correct — Article 222 transfer by President, binding CJI consultation post-Second Judges Case (1993). Statement 2 is correct, so it is NOT the answer.

Statement 3 is incorrect — HC judges have full security of tenure; removal requires a parliamentary address process identical to SC judges. Executive removal without Parliament is constitutionally impermissible.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 deploys the classic entity-swap trap: the correct principle (non-voted salaries protect judicial independence) is retained but the wrong fund is named. 'Consolidated Fund of India' applies to SC judges; 'State Consolidated Fund' applies to HC judges. Students who recall 'judges' salaries are charged to Consolidated Fund' without precision on which fund will mark Statement 1 as correct, falling into the trap. This is one of the most consistently tested distinctions between SC and HC judicial independence provisions.
solution.final_explanation:
The independence of HC judges is protected through salary arrangements, transfer rules, and removal safeguards.

• Statement 1 — NOT Correct: HC judges' salaries are charged to the Consolidated Fund of the State, not the Consolidated Fund of India (which is for SC judges and other Union expenditures). The 'charged' nature (non-votable) correctly describes the protection mechanism, but the entity — Union vs. State — is wrong. This is the entity-swap trap.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Article 222 authorises the President to transfer HC judges, in consultation with the CJI. Post the Second Judges Case (1993), the CJI's opinion (formed collegially) is binding on the President — the transfer cannot be made in opposition to the CJI's view.
• Statement 3 — NOT Correct: HC judges enjoy strong security of tenure. Removal follows the identical procedure as SC judge removal — an address by both Houses of Parliament in the same session, passed with a special majority, followed by a Presidential order. The executive (Council of Ministers) cannot direct the removal of HC judges.

Value Addition:
• The Second Judges Case (1993) established binding collegium consultation — the First Judges Case (1982) had held consultation to be merely advisory.
• A HC judge facing misconduct inquiry may be asked to voluntarily resign — but absent voluntary resignation, the full parliamentary removal process is required.
• Post-transfer, an HC judge's seniority and benefits are protected under Article 222(2).

concepts_used: Original Jurisdiction of High Courts

solution.concept_anchor: Court of Record — distinct from original jurisdiction
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students may think that 'inherent power to punish for contempt' is a separate power from Court of Record status, placing it in the 'odd one out' category, when in reality it is a direct consequence of Court of Record status.
elimination_logic: Identify the common attribute: options (a), (c), and (d) are all consequences or characteristics of a HC being a Court of Record under Article 215.
Option (a) — judgments having permanent evidentiary value: direct consequence of Court of Record status.
Option (c) — inherent power to punish for contempt: direct and primary consequence of Court of Record status under Article 215.
Option (d) — records cannot be questioned in collateral proceedings in subordinate courts: a defining feature of Court of Record status.

Option (b) — power to try original civil suits above a specified pecuniary value: this is original jurisdiction belonging only to Charter HCs, not a feature of Court of Record status. (b) is the odd one out.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges 'Court of Record' with 'original jurisdiction.' Students who associate HCs generally with broad powers may include original jurisdiction as part of Court of Record attributes. In reality, being a Court of Record is about the evidentiary weight of decisions, the inviolability of records, and contempt power — not about trial jurisdiction. Original civil jurisdiction is an entirely separate attribute possessed only by three Charter HCs, completely independent of Court of Record status.
solution.final_explanation:
Court of Record status under Article 215 has specific and defined consequences — original civil jurisdiction is not among them.

• Option (a): Characteristic of Court of Record — judgments of a Court of Record have permanent evidentiary value; they are treated as conclusive evidence of what transpired.
• Option (b): NOT a characteristic of Court of Record — this describes original civil jurisdiction, which belongs only to the three Charter HCs (Calcutta, Bombay, Madras). All HCs are Courts of Record, but not all have original civil jurisdiction. This is the odd one out.
• Option (c): Characteristic of Court of Record — the power to punish for contempt of court is a direct and primary consequence of Court of Record status under Article 215.
• Option (d): Characteristic of Court of Record — records of a Court of Record are so inviolable that they cannot be questioned, disputed, or contradicted in any subordinate court or collateral proceeding.

Value Addition:
• Court of Record status applies to both the HC (Article 215) and SC (Article 129) — both have constitutional contempt powers.
• The Contempt of Courts Act 1971 supplements but does not replace the constitutional contempt power of Courts of Record.
• Being a Court of Record historically referred to courts whose records were conclusive evidence of proceedings — a concept inherited from English common law.

concepts_used: High Court's Jurisdiction over Subordinate Courts: Control and Inspection

solution.concept_anchor: Article 235 — HC controls subordinate courts; Article 233 — Governor appoints
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know the Governor makes appointments of district judges (Article 233) may conflate appointment powers with control powers, and choose 'Governor' for the blank.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (b): The Governor appoints district judges under Article 233, but Article 235 vests control (service matters, posting, promotion, leave) in the HC — not the Governor.
Eliminate (c): State Public Service Commissions are involved in recruitment to judicial service below district judge level (Article 234), not in day-to-day control of subordinate judiciary.
Eliminate (d): The Law Minister has no constitutional role in the control of subordinate courts — this is an executive encroachment the Constitution specifically prevents.
Confirm (a): Article 235 — control over district courts and subordinate courts in service matters is vested in the High Court.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap substitutes 'Governor' for 'High Court.' Students who recall the Governor's role in district judge appointments (Article 233) may incorrectly extend this to the control of subordinate courts in service matters (Article 235). The constitutional design deliberately separates these two functions: appointment is by the Governor (with HC consultation), while ongoing control/service matters are with the HC — a nuanced division that is a recurring UPSC topic.
solution.final_explanation:
The control of subordinate judiciary is carefully allocated in the Constitution to prevent executive interference with judicial administration.

• Option (a): Correct. Article 235 vests control over district courts and subordinate courts — in matters of posting, promotion, grant of leave, and other service conditions — in the High Court. This ensures judicial independence from the executive in day-to-day judicial administration.
• Option (b): Incorrect. The Governor appoints district judges under Article 233, but this appointment power does not extend to control over service matters after appointment — that is the HC's domain.
• Option (c): Incorrect. The State Public Service Commission is involved in initial recruitment to the subordinate judicial service below district judge level (Article 234), not in ongoing control of posted judicial officers.
• Option (d): Incorrect. The Law Minister has no constitutional role in the control of subordinate courts — any executive role in judicial service matters would compromise judicial independence, which the Constitution prevents through Article 235.

Value Addition:
• The HC's control under Article 235 is comprehensive — even matters like medical leave of judicial officers require HC approval.
• State governments sometimes dispute the HC's control in disciplinary matters, leading to constitutional litigation.
• The Governor's appointment power (Article 233) requires consultation with the HC — making the HC influential in both appointment and control, though through different constitutional mechanisms.

solution.concept_anchor: Whirlpool Corp — Article 226 cannot be ousted by legislation
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who recall that HCs can refuse writ petitions on discretionary grounds may mistakenly conclude that legislation can also bar HC writ jurisdiction, making (a) appear plausible.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): While HCs can discretionarily refuse writs (e.g., for delay, alternative remedy), this is different from saying 'Parliament can oust HC writ jurisdiction by ordinary legislation' — the Whirlpool Corp case (1998) held this is not permissible.
Eliminate (b): Article 226 jurisdiction extends to private bodies performing public functions — the pair incorrectly states it is confined to 'government bodies and statutory authorities' only.
Eliminate (d): Article 226 is not suspended during National Emergency — unlike Article 32. The pair is factually wrong on the Emergency suspension.

Confirm (c): The HC has discretion to refuse writ relief if the petitioner has an equally efficacious alternative remedy available — this is a well-established principle under Article 226 that makes this pair correctly matched.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) uses a partial-truth trap: it correctly notes that HC writ jurisdiction can be exercised 'discretionarily' (true) but then adds that 'Parliament can oust it by ordinary legislation' (false per Whirlpool Corp). The two parts of the statement look coherent — if HCs can discretionarily refuse, perhaps Parliament can mandate refusal — but the constitutional reality is that judicial discretion is different from legislative ouster, and the latter is impermissible.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 226 writ jurisdiction has both a broad scope and defined limitations — but legislative ouster is not among those limitations.

• Option (a): Incorrectly matched — while HCs have discretion to refuse writs, Parliament cannot oust HC writ jurisdiction under Article 226 by ordinary legislation. The Whirlpool Corporation v. Registrar of Trade Marks (1998) case settled this conclusively — HC jurisdiction under Article 226 cannot be excluded by statute.
• Option (b): Incorrectly matched — Article 226 writs can be issued against private bodies that discharge public functions, not just government bodies and statutory authorities. This is a judicially expanded scope.
• Option (c): Correctly matched — the HC has inherent discretion under Article 226 to refuse writ relief when an equally efficacious alternative remedy exists. However, this discretion is exercised case by case — it does not bar the petition automatically.
• Option (d): Incorrectly matched — Article 226 is not suspended during a National Emergency. Only Article 32 (the right to move the Supreme Court for FR enforcement) can be suspended under Article 359 during Emergency. Article 226 continues to operate.

Value Addition:
• The 'alternative remedy' bar is discretionary, not jurisdictional — the HC can still exercise jurisdiction despite the existence of an alternative remedy in exceptional cases.
• Fraud on a statutory authority, breach of natural justice, and patent arbitrariness are grounds where HCs entertain Article 226 petitions despite statutory alternatives.
• The Whirlpool Corp principle is frequently applied to protect HC jurisdiction when statutes contain ouster clauses.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 228 — HC withdraws subordinate court case on constitutional question

statement_analysis.statement: In a second civil appeal before a High Court, the HC may reopen and re-examine concurrent findings of fact if it is of the view that the lower courts committed a grave error of appreciation of evidence.
statement_analysis.reason: Second appeals before the HC are confined to substantial questions of law — concurrent findings of fact are ordinarily binding and cannot be re-examined even for perceived errors of evidence appreciation.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 228 empowers the High Court to withdraw a case from a subordinate court when a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution arises in that case.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 228 specifically enables HC withdrawal of cases from subordinate courts when a substantial constitutional interpretation question arises — the HC then decides the constitutional question and may either dispose the case or return it to the lower court.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 139A, the Supreme Court can transfer cases pending before one High Court to another High Court when cases involving the same or substantially similar questions of law are pending.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 139A expressly empowers the SC to transfer cases from one HC to another (or to itself) when substantial questions of law of general importance are involved and similar cases are pending in different HCs.

statement_analysis.statement: A High Court has power under Article 139A to transfer a case pending before a Sessions Court to another state's Sessions Court when common constitutional questions are involved.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 139A is a Supreme Court power — the HC has no power under Article 139A to transfer cases between courts. The HC's transfer/withdrawal power is under Article 228, which covers withdrawal from subordinate courts within its own jurisdiction only.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know Article 139A exists and that HCs have case transfer/withdrawal powers may conflate them, treating Statement 4 as correct and elevating the count to three.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is incorrect — second appeal is limited to questions of law; concurrent findings of fact are binding on the HC. Eliminate counts treating Statement 1 as correct.
Statement 2 is correct — Article 228 is exactly this: HC withdrawal of subordinate court cases on constitutional interpretation questions.
Statement 3 is correct — Article 139A is the SC's transfer power across HCs — accurately described.

Statement 4 is incorrect — Article 139A vests in the SC, not the HC. HCs have no power under Article 139A, and Article 228 covers only withdrawal to the HC itself, not inter-state transfers. Only Statements 2 and 3 are correct — answer is (a) Only two.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 deploys a temporal-swap-adjacent entity-swap: it correctly identifies the subject matter (transfer of cases involving constitutional questions) but attributes the Article 139A power to the HC rather than the SC. Students who know that HCs have withdrawal powers (Article 228) and that Article 139A exists may conflate the two, incorrectly attributing the SC's Article 139A power to the HC. The trap is more precisely an entity-swap — swapping the constitutional entity that holds the power.
solution.final_explanation:
Case transfer and withdrawal powers in the constitutional scheme are carefully allocated.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: HC's second appellate jurisdiction under Section 100 CPC is confined to substantial questions of law — concurrent factual findings of two lower courts are binding on the HC regardless of the HC's own assessment of the evidence.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Article 228 is the HC's specific power to withdraw from a subordinate court any case in which a substantial question of constitutional interpretation arises. After deciding the constitutional question, the HC may dispose the case or return it to the subordinate court with its determination.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 139A (inserted by 42nd Amendment, 1976) vests in the Supreme Court the power to transfer cases from one HC to another HC, or from any HC to itself, when similar constitutional questions are pending in multiple HCs.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Article 139A is an SC power — the HC has no power under it. The HC's withdrawal power (Article 228) is confined to cases before its own subordinate courts, not across states. Attributing Article 139A powers to the HC is an entity-swap error.

Value Addition:
• Under Article 228, after the HC decides the constitutional question, it sends the case back with a copy of its judgment to the subordinate court for disposal.
• Article 139A transfer can be initiated by the SC suo motu or on petition by a party.
• Transfer petitions under Article 139A often arise in high-profile criminal cases where fair trial concerns exist.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 32 is a fundamental right; Article 226 is not
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is A correct? — Yes. Article 32 is guaranteed under Part III as a Fundamental Right — the right to constitutional remedies is itself a fundamental right, making it non-negotiable and directly enforceable.

Step 2: Is R correct? — Yes. Unlike Article 32, Article 226 does not carry the guarantee of a fundamental right — it is a discretionary constitutional power of the HC. The HC can, in its discretion, refuse to exercise writ jurisdiction on grounds like delay, alternative remedy, or laches. This is a well-settled distinction.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. The reason that Article 226 is discretionary does not explain why Article 32 is a Fundamental Right. A is about Article 32's status as a FR; R is about Article 226's discretionary nature — these are independent facts about two different articles. R is a contrast to A, not a causal explanation of A.
A correct + R correct + R does NOT causally explain A → option (b). Confirm: correct_option is (b).
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests precise understanding of the relationship between Article 32 and Article 226, and whether one's status as a FR explains the other's discretionary character.

Assertion (A): Correct. Article 32 is placed within Part III (Fundamental Rights) and is itself a Fundamental Right — Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul of the Constitution.' Being a FR, it cannot be refused by the Supreme Court — the Court must entertain petitions under Article 32 when a FR violation is alleged.

Reason (R): Correct. Article 226 is a constitutional power of the HC, not a Fundamental Right. Consequently, the HC has discretion to refuse writ relief — on grounds of delay, availability of alternative remedy, laches, or abuse of process. This discretion is well-recognised in HC writ jurisprudence.

Causal link: R correctly describes the HC's discretionary character but does not explain why Article 32 is a Fundamental Right. These are two independent propositions about two different articles. The answer is (b) — both A and R are correct but R is not the explanation of A.

Value Addition:
• The SC under Article 32 cannot refuse to entertain a petition if a FR violation is alleged — unlike the HC under Article 226.
• Article 359 allows suspension of the right to move courts for FR enforcement (including Article 32) during Emergency — but not Article 226.
• Both articles permit the same five types of writs: habeas corpus, mandamus, certiorari, prohibition, quo warranto.

solution.concept_anchor: Articles 217, 222, 223, 224 — distinct HC judge provisions
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who confuse Article 222 (transfer of judges) with Article 223 (Acting CJ) may swap their placements in the matching, choosing option (c).
elimination_logic: Match A (Article 217) with 2 — Article 217 covers the appointment of HC judges by the President in consultation with CJI, HC Chief Justice, and Governor.
Match B (Article 222) with 4 — Article 222 specifically governs transfer of HC judges from one HC to another by Presidential order in consultation with CJI.
Match C (Article 223) with 1 — Article 223 deals with the appointment of an Acting Chief Justice of an HC when the CJ post is vacant or CJ is unable to perform duties.

Match D (Article 224) with 3 — Article 224 authorises appointment of Additional and Acting Judges to handle temporary increase in work (maximum 2 years). Correct matching: A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3 = option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap targets Articles 222 and 223 — both involve the CJ-related provisions of HCs. Article 222 (transfer) and Article 223 (Acting Chief Justice) are adjacent provisions dealing with different situations: one is about moving a judge across HCs, the other about filling the CJ role temporarily. Students who have a vague recall of these two articles may swap them, placing Article 222 in the Acting CJ row and Article 223 in the transfer row — a common examination error.
solution.final_explanation:
Four constitutional articles govern different aspects of HC judicial personnel.

Correct pairings:
• A–2: Article 217 governs the appointment of HC judges — by the President in consultation with the CJI, the Chief Justice of the HC, and the Governor of the state. This is the foundational appointment provision.
• B–4: Article 222 specifically provides for the transfer of HC judges from one HC to another by the President, acting in consultation with the CJI (binding consultation post-Second Judges Case).
• C–1: Article 223 empowers the President to appoint an Acting Chief Justice of a HC whenever the office of the Chief Justice is vacant or when the Chief Justice is unable to perform duties due to absence or otherwise.
• D–3: Article 224 authorises the appointment of Additional Judges (for up to two years) and Acting Judges to handle temporary increases in the workload of an HC. Additional judges cannot be automatically confirmed as permanent judges.

The trap pairings are B–1 (confusing transfer with Acting CJ) and C–4 (the reverse).

Value Addition:
• Article 224A (retired judge appointments) is distinct from Article 224 (Additional/Acting Judges) — Article 224A requires consent of both President and the retired judge.
• Article 217(2) specifies qualification criteria for HC judges — advocate of HC for 10 years or a judicial officer.
• The Governor's role under Article 217 (consultation in appointment) distinguishes HC from SC judge appointments.

solution.concept_anchor: HC PIL — territorial nexus required even in public interest
solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know HCs can issue directions to government on governance matters through PIL may choose (d), not recognising the absence of territorial nexus as the decisive barrier.
elimination_logic: Identify the legal issue: An environmental NGO in Mumbai files a PIL before the Bombay HC challenging a dam project in Uttarakhand, alleging it affects national biodiversity.
Eliminate (a): The Bombay HC does entertain PILs on environmental matters — this is not the barrier; the barrier is territorial nexus.
Eliminate (b): PILs don't require personal aggrievement — but this is not the issue here; locus standi is not what fails.

Eliminate (d): Even genuine public interest does not override the HC's territorial jurisdictional limits — the Bombay HC cannot issue directions about a project in Uttarakhand that has no cause of action or effect within Maharashtra.

Confirm (c): The Bombay HC lacks territorial jurisdiction over a dam project exclusively located in and affecting Uttarakhand — the PIL should be filed before the Uttarakhand HC or the Supreme Court (which has pan-India reach under Article 32).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap places a genuine environmental issue (biodiversity impact of a dam) within a PIL filed before the wrong HC — the Bombay HC for a project in Uttarakhand. Students who know PIL relaxes locus standi may assume it also relaxes territorial jurisdiction, particularly when the subject involves national biodiversity (which sounds non-territorial). The trap exploits the generality of 'national interest' to override the specificity of territorial jurisdiction — which it does not.
solution.final_explanation:
PIL under Article 226 relaxes the requirement of personal aggrievement (locus standi) but does not relax the HC's territorial jurisdiction.

The scenario: A Mumbai-based NGO files a PIL before the Bombay HC challenging a dam in Uttarakhand on grounds of biodiversity impact.

Applicable principle: The HC's territorial jurisdiction under Article 226 requires that either (i) the cause of action arises within its territory, or (ii) the authority against which relief is sought functions within its territory. A dam project entirely located in Uttarakhand, authorised and monitored by Uttarakhand government/central bodies not operating in Maharashtra, generates no territorial nexus with the Bombay HC.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Bombay HC has full PIL jurisdiction in environmental matters — the issue is not the subject matter but the territorial nexus.
• Option (b): Incorrect. PIL does not require personal aggrievement — locus standi is not the failing here.
• Option (c): Correct. The Bombay HC cannot entertain this PIL because no cause of action and no government authority linked to this project operates within Maharashtra. The proper forum is the Uttarakhand HC (territorial nexus) or the Supreme Court (pan-India jurisdiction under Article 32).
• Option (d): Incorrect. National biodiversity impact does not transform a geographically specific project into one within Bombay HC's territory.

Value Addition:
• PIL petitioners sometimes file before the SC under Article 32 to avoid territorial jurisdiction issues — SC PIL has pan-India effect.
• Courts have cautioned against 'forum shopping' in PILs — filing before a convenient HC without genuine territorial nexus.
• For multi-state environmental projects, the SC is often the appropriate forum — its directions bind all states uniformly.

solution.concept_anchor: Section 482 CrPC inherent power — complement to Article 226/227

statement_analysis.statement: The inherent power of the High Court preserved under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (now the Bhartiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita) is a constitutional power flowing from Articles 226 and 227.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 482 CrPC inherent powers are statutory in basis — they preserve powers the HC possesses as a superior court of record. While they complement Articles 226/227, they are not themselves constitutional powers; they are statutory powers exercised by a constitutional court.

statement_analysis.statement: A High Court can exercise its inherent power under Section 482 CrPC to quash criminal proceedings even before the framing of charges, provided it is necessary to prevent abuse of the process of the court.
statement_analysis.reason: Inherent power under Section 482 CrPC allows the HC to quash FIRs and criminal proceedings at any stage — including pre-charge — if continuation would amount to abuse of process or miscarriage of justice.

statement_analysis.statement: Inherent powers of the High Court under Section 482 CrPC cannot be exercised to circumvent an express statutory provision that specifically bars the court from entertaining an application.
statement_analysis.reason: Courts have consistently held that inherent powers operate in areas not specifically covered by statute — they cannot be used to override or circumvent express statutory bars or specific provisions. Inherent powers fill gaps; they do not override enacted law.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know that inherent powers are wide and complementary to constitutional powers may accept Statement 1 as correct, confusing the constitutional basis of the HC's status with the statutory basis of Section 482.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is incorrect — Section 482 powers are statutory (preserved by CrPC), not constitutional. While the HC is a constitutional court and its Court of Record status supports inherent powers, Section 482 itself is a statutory provision. These are different sources.
Statement 2 is correct — pre-charge quashing of FIRs and criminal proceedings is a well-established exercise of inherent power under Section 482.
Statement 3 is correct — inherent powers cannot override express statutory provisions or specific jurisdictional bars. They operate in interstices of statute, not against it.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct, Statement 1 is incorrect — option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap in Statement 1 merges the constitutional source of the HC's character (as a superior Court of Record under Article 215) with the statutory basis of inherent powers (Section 482 CrPC). Students who know that HCs are constitutional courts and that their inherent powers are related to this status may conclude that Section 482 powers are themselves constitutional. The precise position: Section 482 is a statutory preservation of inherent powers that the HC, as a superior court of record, possesses — the authority is inherent, the preservation is statutory.
solution.final_explanation:
The inherent powers of the HC under Section 482 CrPC occupy a distinctive space between constitutional and statutory powers.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Section 482 CrPC preserves the inherent power of the HC as a superior court, but this preservation is by statute, not by the Constitution directly. Articles 226 and 227 are constitutional sources; Section 482 is a statutory provision. While they all reside in the same court and serve complementary purposes, they are distinct in source and scope. Conflating them is the trap.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The HC can quash an FIR or criminal proceedings at any stage — including before charge framing — using Section 482, if the court finds that continuation would abuse process, cause miscarriage of justice, or that the FIR discloses no cognisable offence. This pre-trial quashing is a powerful judicial tool.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Inherent powers fill gaps in procedural law — they operate where statute is silent or incomplete. Where a statute specifically bars a remedy or expressly excludes jurisdiction, inherent powers cannot be used to override that bar.

Value Addition:
• BNSS 2023 (replacing CrPC) preserves inherent powers of HCs — continuity of this power across the legislative change.
• The SC in State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal (1992) laid down exhaustive guidelines for when HC can quash FIRs under Section 482.
• An Article 226 writ petition and a Section 482 application can sometimes be filed together — courts often consolidate hearing.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 329 bars HC writ during elections; post-election petition to HC

statement_analysis.statement: Article 329 of the Constitution bars courts, including High Courts, from interfering in the electoral process once it has commenced — this bar applies even to the High Court's writ jurisdiction under Article 226.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 329 is a constitutional bar that operates regardless of the HC's writ jurisdiction — it bars courts from challenging any electoral step during the ongoing election process. HC writ jurisdiction does not override this constitutional bar.

statement_analysis.statement: The constitutional bar under Article 329 applies equally to disputes regarding the election of the President and Vice-President of India — such disputes must therefore be raised before the High Court after the election is concluded.
statement_analysis.reason: Presidential and Vice-Presidential election disputes are governed by Article 71, not Article 329. Disputes over these elections go exclusively to the Supreme Court — not to any HC. Article 329's bar and the HC's post-election petition jurisdiction do not apply to Presidential/VP election disputes.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know that Article 329 has a broad bar may assume it applies universally including to Presidential elections, and accept Statement 2 as correct, choosing (a).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Article 329 creates a constitutional bar on courts during the election process — this explicitly covers HC writ jurisdiction. Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: Presidential and VP election disputes fall under Article 71 and go to the SC, not any HC. The HC's post-election petition jurisdiction under RPA 1951 does not extend to Presidential/VP elections. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — option (c)... wait: re-check options. (c) is 'Statement 1 is correct but Statement 2 is incorrect.' Correct_option must be (c).

Re-examine: correct_option listed as (b). Re-read options: (a) Both correct, (b) Both incorrect, (c) Statement 1 correct Statement 2 incorrect, (d) Statement 1 incorrect Statement 2 correct. Since Statement 1 is correct and Statement 2 is incorrect, the answer is (c). Correct_option corrected to 'c'.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses scope-extension: students who know Article 329 has a broad bar and that post-election disputes go to the HC may extend this mechanism to Presidential elections — which it does not cover. Presidential and VP elections are governed by an entirely separate constitutional provision (Article 71), and disputes go exclusively to the SC. The HC has no jurisdiction over Presidential/VP election disputes — neither during the election (Article 329 does not specifically mention these) nor after (Article 71 is the exclusive route).
solution.final_explanation:
The relationship between Article 329 (bar on court intervention during elections) and post-election dispute jurisdiction is nuanced.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 329 creates a categorical bar on courts during the ongoing election process. It applies to High Courts including their writ jurisdiction under Article 226. Challenges to electoral steps (polling schedules, nomination decisions, etc.) cannot be made during the election process — the remedy lies after the election through the election petition mechanism.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The HC's post-election jurisdiction under the Representation of the People Act, 1951 covers elections to the state legislature and Lok Sabha — not Presidential or Vice-Presidential elections. Article 71 exclusively vests jurisdiction over Presidential and VP election disputes in the Supreme Court. Extending the HC's election petition jurisdiction to Presidential/VP elections is a constitutionally incorrect scope-extension.

Value Addition:
• Article 329(a) bars challenging election of a person as a member of either House of Parliament or state legislature except by election petition.
• The Election Commission's power to postpone elections is protected from court interference during the election process.
• Under Article 71(3), Parliament has power to legislate for the resolution of Presidential/VP election doubts — leading to the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952.

final_explanation:
The relationship between Article 329 and post-election petition jurisdiction is carefully delineated in the Constitution.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 329 creates an absolute constitutional bar on courts — including HCs exercising writ jurisdiction under Article 226 — from interfering in the election process once it has commenced. The HC cannot, through its writ jurisdiction, halt or review electoral steps during an ongoing election. The post-election election petition is the prescribed remedy.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The HC's jurisdiction over election disputes (under RPA 1951) covers elections to state legislature and Lok Sabha constituencies within its territory. Presidential and Vice-Presidential elections are governed by Article 71 — disputes regarding these elections go exclusively to the Supreme Court of India. Extending the HC's election petition jurisdiction to Presidential/VP elections is constitutionally incorrect.

Value Addition:
• The bar under Article 329 does not prevent post-election scrutiny — it only prevents mid-election judicial intervention.
• Presidential election disputes are heard by a bench of the SC under Article 71(1).
• The RPA 1951 sets a 45-day limitation period for filing election petitions after declaration of results.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 227 extends to tribunals — military tribunals excluded

statement_analysis.statement: The High Court's supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 extends to all courts and tribunals within its territorial jurisdiction, with the express exclusion of courts or tribunals constituted by or under any law relating to the Armed Forces.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 227(4) specifically excludes courts or tribunals constituted under laws relating to the Armed Forces from the HC's supervisory jurisdiction — all other courts and tribunals are covered.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 227 empowers the High Court to call for returns from subordinate courts and tribunals and prescribe forms in which such returns shall be made.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 227(2)(a) expressly enables the HC to call for returns from subordinate courts — this is one of the specific powers articulated in the article as part of the superintendence function.

statement_analysis.statement: The supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 can be used by the High Court to reverse the decision of a lower court on merits, substituting the HC's own assessment of facts in place of the lower court's findings.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 227 supervisory jurisdiction cannot be used to re-examine or reverse decisions on merits — it is confined to correcting jurisdictional errors, perversity, and errors of law apparent on the face of the record. Substituting factual assessments is appellate jurisdiction, which Article 227 does not grant.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know Article 227 is a broad supervisory power may assume it covers merit review too, and mark Statement 3 as correct, choosing option (d) which includes all three.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — Article 227(4) specifically excludes Armed Forces courts/tribunals from HC superintendence. This exclusion is tested frequently.
Statement 2 is correct — Article 227(2)(a) expressly includes power to call for returns from subordinate courts as part of superintendence.

Statement 3 is incorrect — Article 227 is supervisory, not appellate. Merit review and substitution of factual assessments are impermissible under Article 227. Eliminate options including Statement 3 as correct.
Statements 1 and 2 are correct, Statement 3 is incorrect — option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 3 extends Article 227's 'superintendence over all courts' to include merit review of decisions. Students who associate 'superintendence' with comprehensive oversight (as in management) may assume this includes factual review. The constitutional interpretation is precisely the opposite: superintendence under Article 227 is a supervisory check for jurisdictional correctness, not an appellate review of factual findings. The trap is further reinforced by students knowing the HC has broad powers — the word 'all courts' in Article 227 makes Statement 3 plausible.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 227 is a carefully bounded power — 'superintendence' does not mean unlimited oversight.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 227(4) explicitly carves out courts and tribunals constituted under laws relating to the Armed Forces from the HC's supervisory jurisdiction. This is one of the most frequently tested exclusions. All other courts and tribunals (including industrial tribunals, revenue courts, etc.) within the HC's territory are subject to superintendence.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Article 227(2) enumerates specific superintendence powers — including calling for returns from subordinate courts, prescribing the forms in which such returns are made, and making rules regarding proceedings. These administrative-supervisory functions are part of the article's express text.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: HC's power under Article 227 does not extend to reversing decisions on merits or substituting its factual findings for those of the lower court. This would be appellate review. Article 227 allows the HC to correct jurisdictional errors, excess of jurisdiction, refusal to exercise jurisdiction, or errors of law so apparent as to be called perverse — but not ordinary factual disagreements.

Value Addition:
• Article 227 review is wider than certiorari (which requires jurisdictional error) but narrower than an appeal (which covers merits).
• HC can suo motu (on its own initiative) exercise Article 227 superintendence — parties need not file a petition.
• Article 235 and Article 227 together give the HC comprehensive control over the subordinate judiciary.
